title: Christmas Traditions in the Dominican Republic: Food, Music, Family
summary: Discover Dominican Christmas traditions, from charamicos and aguinaldos to Nochebuena meals, gift exchanges, and Three Kings Day celebrations.
body_markdown:
**Quick answer:** Christmas traditions in the Dominican Republic include handmade charamico decorations, musical gatherings called aguinaldos, and a family meal on Christmas Eve, or Nochebuena. Gift exchanges and religious celebrations also form part of the season, which can continue through Three Kings Day on January 6. Customs vary between families and communities.


If you have relatives in the Dominican Republic, you’ve probably heard about charamicos, aguinaldos, or a Nochebuena spread that takes all day to prepare. These traditions don’t follow a single script. Every family, town, and generation adds its own touch, blending faith, food, and music into a season that feels both personal and shared.


This guide walks through what the season typically looks like in the Dominican Republic, from early December decorations to the meals served on Christmas Eve, the music that signals the season has arrived, and the gift-giving customs that stretch into January. Whether you’re celebrating with Dominican relatives in the US or want to bring a few of these traditions into your own home, here’s what to know.


## When Is Christmas Celebrated in the Dominican Republic?


Christmas Day falls on December 25 in the Dominican Republic, just as it does across much of the world. But the season itself doesn’t have one fixed starting point. Preparations, decorations, and family gatherings build gradually throughout December, and the pace varies by household and region.


Here’s a simple calendar to help you follow the key dates:


**Date or Period** **Celebration** **What to Know**


Throughout December Christmas preparations Decorations, music, and gatherings build up gradually and vary by family and locality


December 24, 2026 Nochebuena Christmas Eve, centered on an important family meal


December 25, 2026 Navidad Christmas Day


December 31, 2026 Nochevieja New Year’s Eve, a separate celebration from Christmas


January 1, 2027 Año Nuevo New Year’s Day


January 6, 2027 Día de Reyes Three Kings Day, associated with gift-giving in some families


It’s worth noting that Nochevieja and Año Nuevo are their own distinct celebrations, separate from the Christmas traditions that precede them. And while this calendar gives you dates to plan around, it isn’t a schedule of business closures or a fixed itinerary—it’s simply a guide to when each celebration typically falls.


## Charamicos: A Distinctive Dominican Christmas Decoration


One of the most recognizable symbols of the season is the charamico, a handmade decoration constructed from small, dry branches. Dominican families shape these branches into trees, stars, and other figures, often displaying them alongside string lights, Christmas trees, and Nativity scenes. The craftsmanship behind each piece reflects a tradition passed down through generations of[Dominican charamico decorations](https://academia.org.do/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/BOLETIN-DIGITAL-DE-LA-ACADEMIA-DOMINICANA-DE-LA-LENGUA-DE-ENERO-DE-2026.pdf) , as documented by the Dominican Academy of Language.


## What Are Dominican Christmas Aguinaldos?


### Musical Visits from House to House


An aguinaldo, in the Dominican Christmas context, is a gathering in which a group of people visits homes singing and playing Christmas music together. Hosts often welcome these visitors with ginger tea or hot chocolate, turning the impromptu performance into a shared moment of warmth. This practice remains active in some communities, particularly among religious groups, though it has become less common elsewhere as traditions shift with each generation. According to Diario Libre, sociologist Carlos Andújar described the aguinaldo as a blend of musical traditions: the tambora and güiro accompany popular merengue songs in what he calls a cultural mix between Spanish influences and traditions created within the Dominican Republic itself, a fusion reflected in[the tradition of Dominican Christmas aguinaldos](https://www.diariolibre.com/revista/buena-vida/2023/12/23/descubre-las-tradiciones-navidenas-dominicanas/2559602) .


### Merengue and Familiar Seasonal Songs


Music plays a central role in Dominican Christmas celebrations, filling homes and neighborhood gatherings alike. Among the most recognizable seasonal songs is “Volvió Juanita,” performed by merengue artist Milly Quezada. The song is closely associated with the holiday because it tells the story of a Dominican woman living abroad who returns home each Christmas, carrying hopes, dreams, and gifts for her loved ones. For many Dominican families, hearing this song on the radio is a seasonal signal that the holidays have truly begun—a reminder of how closely the season is tied to reuniting with family, wherever they may be living.


## Nochebuena: Gathering for Christmas Eve


Nochebuena, meaning Christmas Eve, centers on a shared family meal and the gathering of loved ones. For many families, this is the one night of the year when relatives make a point of traveling back to their hometowns, and some who live overseas plan their return trips specifically around this date.


Religious observance is part of the evening for some families, who attend a Christmas service such as Misa de Gallo, though this practice isn’t universal and varies by household and by faith tradition. Not every family follows the same religious schedule or meal timing, and that’s part of what makes the holiday feel personal rather than formulaic. The emphasis on togetherness and hospitality that defines so much of Dominican culture extends naturally into[family gatherings during the Dominican Christmas season](https://www.godominicanrepublic.com/about-our-country) , according to the country’s official tourism site, which highlights the importance Dominicans place on connecting with loved ones and visitors alike.


## What Do People Eat at Christmas in the Dominican Republic?


Dominican Christmas food varies from household to household, shaped by family recipes, regional preferences, and budget. There’s no single official menu, but certain dishes appear often enough to be considered staples of[foods served at Dominican Nochebuena celebrations](https://www.kariculture.net/es/navidad-republica-dominicana-sus-tradiciones/) .


**Food or Drink** **What It Is**


Cerdo asado or lechón asado Roast pork, often the centerpiece of the Nochebuena table


Moro de guandules Rice cooked with pigeon peas


Pasteles en hoja Filled preparations wrapped in leaves, with recipes varying by household


Ensalada rusa A mixed salad with variations from family to family


Telera Bread that may accompany the holiday meal


Ponche A festive drink whose recipes may contain alcohol


Some families prepare roast chicken instead of pork, and plenty of households adjust recipes based on what fits their taste and their budget that year. What stays consistent isn’t the exact dish list but the spirit behind it: cooking together, sharing memories tied to specific recipes, and gathering around a table that reflects each family’s own version of the holiday.


## Angelitos and Three Kings Day Gifts


### Angelito Gift Exchanges


An angelito is a gift exchange tradition practiced among relatives, friends, or coworkers, similar in spirit to a Secret Santa exchange familiar to many US readers. Participants typically draw names and agree on a spending budget ahead of time, though the specific rules, timing, and amount vary from one group to the next. Some families organize their angelito early in December, while others save the exchange for a gathering closer to Christmas itself.


### Día de Reyes on January 6


Three Kings Day, observed on January 6, commemorates the visit of the Three Kings and is associated with gift-giving for children in some Dominican families. That said, gift-giving traditions aren’t limited to this one date. Santa Claus and Christmas Day gifts also feature prominently in many households, and the balance between the two varies by family. Not every child receives gifts exclusively on January 6, and some families incorporate both traditions into their celebrations.


## How to Celebrate Dominican Christmas Traditions in the US


Living far from the Dominican Republic doesn’t mean you have to leave these traditions behind. Here are a few practical ways to bring them into your home:


- **Prepare a family recipe.** Ask relatives about their specific version of a dish like moro de guandules or pasteles en hoja, and note the small details that make it theirs.
- **Build a playlist.** Include the songs that carry meaning for your family, whether that’s merengue classics or a specific artist tied to your childhood memories.
- **Display charamicos or other meaningful decorations.** Even a simple handmade touch can connect your home to the traditions your family grew up with.
- **Organize an angelito exchange.** Set an agreed budget with family or friends to keep the tradition fun and low-pressure.
- **Schedule a video call during the gathering.** If relatives in the Dominican Republic are celebrating Nochebuena, a call can help bridge the distance.
- **Share the meaning behind these dates with younger relatives.** Explaining why Nochebuena or Three Kings Day matters helps keep the tradition alive for the next generation.


There’s no single correct way to celebrate. Traditions can adapt to life abroad while still holding onto the family significance that makes them worth keeping.

## Frequently Asked Questions


**How is Christmas celebrated in the Dominican Republic?** Christmas in the Dominican Republic typically includes decorations like charamicos, musical gatherings called aguinaldos, and a family meal on Nochebuena, or Christmas Eve. Some families also attend religious services, and the season often extends through gift-giving on Three Kings Day in January. Specific customs vary by family and region.


**What are charamicos?** Charamicos are handmade Christmas decorations crafted from small, dry branches, shaped into forms like trees and stars. They’re often displayed alongside lights, Christmas trees, and Nativity scenes. The tradition reflects a distinctly Dominican approach to holiday decorating.


**What are Dominican Christmas aguinaldos?** Aguinaldos are gatherings in which groups of people visit homes singing and playing Christmas music, often accompanied by instruments like the tambora and güiro. Hosts may offer refreshments such as ginger tea or hot chocolate. The tradition remains active in some communities, especially among religious groups, though it’s less common in others.


**What do Dominican families eat on Christmas Eve?** Common Nochebuena dishes include roast pork (cerdo asado or lechón asado), moro de guandules, pasteles en hoja, ensalada rusa, telera bread, and ponche. Some families substitute roast chicken, and recipes vary widely based on household preference and budget.


**What is an angelito gift exchange?** An angelito is a gift exchange among relatives, friends, or coworkers, similar to a Secret Santa. Participants typically agree on a budget in advance, though the specific rules and timing vary by group.


**When do children receive Christmas gifts?** Dominican children may receive gifts from Santa Claus on Christmas Day, from family during Three Kings Day on January 6, or both, depending on family tradition. There’s no single rule that applies to every household.


**How do you say “Merry Christmas” in the Dominican Republic?** The phrase is “¡Feliz Navidad!”, the same greeting used throughout the Spanish-speaking world.
